tytul: Switching Isn't a Breakup: How to Switch Therapists, Online or Off
tresc_html:
How long have you been rehearsing the switching conversation in the shower? You've drafted the email three times, and every version still opens with "I hope this finds you well," as if your therapist were a supplier you're replacing. On the platform, the option to change your therapist has been opened and closed so many times you could find it with your eyes shut. And under all of it sits a very specific guilt, the kind you'd feel leaving someone at a gas station and driving off.

Why switching feels so much bigger than it is

Therapy is a lopsided relationship, and that's on purpose. You do most of the talking, you bring the parts of your life you don't show anyone else, and your therapist listens without handing over much of their own. So leaving feels like walking away from someone close, even though for your therapist, clients moving on is an ordinary part of the job. They've been through it before, and they'll go through it again.

Then there's the fear of starting from zero. Months of sessions start to look like time and money you'll never get back, and "did I waste all that?" makes staying feel safer than it is. Who sits across from you does matter, though less than the internet likes to suggest, and the research on that is part of what to look for in the next one. Wanting a better match is a reasonable response to that evidence, and there's nothing disloyal in it.

Disclaimer: switching therapists is not a review you leave. Nobody gets one star, and nobody has to read it out loud.

You're changing providers, and that's all a switch has to mean.

How to switch therapists, depending on where you are:

First, a quick check that this is a switch and not a bad month. A few signs you're ready to switch, and not just tired:

  • You can say what you want done differently in one sentence, beyond "something feels off."
  • You've already raised it with your therapist, and nothing changed afterward.
  • Sessions have turned into a recap of your week, and you leave knowing more about your Tuesday than about yourself.
  • The thought has stayed with you for weeks, through the good sessions as well as the bad ones.

If you're not there yet, there's a separate guide on how to tell a bad fit from a rough patch, including what to say to your current therapist first. If you are, here's how the switch itself works.

On an online platform

Most platforms let you request a new match in your account settings or through support. Before you tap anything, look up three things in the platform's own help pages: whether your current therapist gets notified, whether your message history moves over to the new person, and whether the change affects your plan or what you pay. The answers differ from one service to the next, and they're easier to read before you switch than to discover after.

In private practice or a clinic

Outside an app, the cleanest exit is usually one closing session, or a short email if talking feels impossible. The exact wording lives in the guide on fit, so here's only the logistics. Ask your therapist for a referral, because therapists tend to know who in their network works differently than they do. And if you're in a group practice or a clinic, ask whether you can move to someone else in the same place, which often keeps your paperwork and billing where they already are. If the switch changes what you pay, you have more options than the first price you see.

A switch is also different from stopping. Ending therapy on purpose is its own conversation, and this isn't it.

What research turned up:

In 2025, Miggiels and colleagues published a trial in the Journal of Affective Disorders that put this exact worry to the test. They worked with 163 adults with depression in specialized mental health care in the Netherlands, people whose first 16 sessions of therapy hadn't helped enough. Each person was randomly assigned to one of three paths: stay with the same therapist, switch to a new therapist, or switch to a new therapist and a different method. Everyone was offered another 16 sessions over eight weeks.

All three groups improved a little, and none did better or worse than the others. Switching and staying came out about even, so a switch is simply another way to keep going.

The honest limits: this was depression, in specialized clinics in one country, and people were given a path by chance instead of choosing it. Someone who switches because they know exactly what was missing may be in a different position, and this trial can't tell us whether that helps.

That's where your own preferences come in. In 2018, Swift and colleagues pooled studies on client preferences in the Journal of Clinical Psychology and found that clients who got the kind of therapy they preferred were less likely to drop out. So the most useful thing you can bring to a switch is a clear idea of what you want.

And nobody has studied how it feels to request a new therapist at 11 p.m. The data is about outcomes, not about the guilt.

Before you book the next person, do these four things:

  1. Write down what you want done differently. One line each for pace, structure and style. "More homework, less nodding" counts as a requirement, and so does "please stop me when I spend 10 minutes on my landlord." A list like that turns a vague sense that something was missing into something the next person can actually work with.
  2. Save what you already learned. Before you leave, write down the sentences that stuck, the tools that worked and the moments that changed something. Do it now, while you still remember the good sessions as well as the last awkward one, because memory likes to grade the whole course by its final week. Saving what each session gave you is a habit worth keeping with the next therapist too.
  3. Ask for a treatment summary. Your current therapist can write a short one, or your new therapist can request records with your written permission. You don't need the whole file to start well.
  4. Don't judge the new person by session one. A first session with someone new is often heavy, because you're retelling hard things to a stranger. Feeling wrung out the next day is usually the heavy day after a hard session, not proof you chose wrong.
[FEATURE: health-check | The same short questions about the working relationship, answered a few times, so the list you take to the next therapist rests on more than one hard Tuesday.]

When you book, one sentence does most of the work: "I'm switching from another therapist, and I know what didn't work for me. Can we talk about that in the first session?" Most therapists will hear that as useful information, because it is.

You're not starting over. You're starting better informed.

This is what MindSync's Therapy relationship check is for. Answer it after the last few sessions: how safe you feel being honest, how well your therapist understands what you're going through, and whether the work feels like it's going somewhere. Log the one thing you kept wishing your therapist would do in the open answer at the end. Give it time, and your Therapy timeline lines those checks up so you can see whether this is one bad month or the same note for half a year. Then take that list into the first call with the next person, and read it out if you need to.

What's the one thing you'd want your next therapist to know about what didn't work last time?

[FEATURES: Switching without losing the thread || timeline | Months of sessions and realizations on one line, readable in 10 minutes before the first call with someone new. || summaries | A monthly read of what you worked on, which is a better handover than trying to remember it all in the first hour. || goals | What you came to therapy for, in your own words, so the new person hears the target and not just the history.]

Frequently asked questions

What should I do if my BetterHelp therapist isn't the right fit?

You can ask BetterHelp to match you with a different therapist: its FAQ says that if your therapist isn't a good fit, you may elect to be matched to someone else. Before you request it, write down in a line or two what you want done differently, so the new match rests on more than one bad week. Check the help pages for what happens to your message history.

Is it rude to switch therapists?

No, switching therapists isn't rude. It's a normal part of therapy, and therapists expect some clients to move on. A short closing session or a brief message is a considerate way to leave, but you don't owe a long explanation. Asking for a referral or a treatment summary is a reasonable request, too.

Will switching therapists set me back?

Switching therapists doesn't seem to set people back, based on the best evidence so far. In a 2025 trial in the Journal of Affective Disorders, adults with depression who hadn't improved enough and switched therapists did about as well as those who stayed. The study covered depression in Dutch clinics, so it can't speak for every situation.

How many times is it OK to switch therapists?

There's no fixed limit on how many times you can switch therapists. What matters more is whether each switch is based on something you can name. If you notice you leave every therapist at the same point, for example when sessions start getting uncomfortable, that pattern is worth raising with the next one, because it may be part of the work.

Can I switch therapists within the same practice?

Yes, many group practices and clinics let you switch to another therapist in the same place. You usually ask the front desk, the intake coordinator or your current therapist. Staying in the same practice can keep records and billing simpler. It's fine to say you'd like someone with a different approach and ask who might suit you better.
